To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we identified over 7000 host proteins that are differentially expressed upon Vpr induction in an HIV-1 model system and over 28,000 host phospho-proteins whose abundance was altered upon Vpr induction.
we developed a new model system to investigate the effects of HIV-1 Vpr on the host proteome, and we found evidence of Vpr affecting the activity of SRPKs, suggesting a role in RNA splicing.
we identified and quantified the abundance of 7,000 host proteins and 28K phospho-peptides and observed Vpr-mediated effects on cell cycle proteins and splicing proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of host targets of viral protein Vpr, and the corresponding modulation in the phosphorylation status of down-stream pathways.
the identification of cellular proteins that are targeted by HIV-1 accessory proteins and the modulation of their PTMs.
the identification of cellular targets and their PTMs, which are modulated by HIV-1 accessory proteins, and the impact on the viral replication cycle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study provides a novel inducible model of HIV-1 that can be used to study the mechanisms of HIV-1 accessory proteins.

the results of this study provide insight into the mechanisms of action of HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr, specifically the modulation of cellular protein phosphorylation, which is a major post-translational modification that plays a role in the regulation of cellular processes and pathways.
this study provides a data-resource and a new experimental system for future studies to validate host proteins and phosphorylations affected by HIV- 1 and its accessory proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we identified 7,000 host proteins and 28K phospho-peptides that are affected by Vpr, including 2,000 proteins that are phosphorylated.
we have identified 7000 host proteins whose abundance and 28,500 phosphorylation sites whose activity are altered in response to the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr.

we developed a new experimental system to study HIV-1 accessory protein function and applied quantitative mass-spectrometry-based techniques to identify the host proteins affected by the HIV-1 accessory proteins Vpr and Nef.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Vpr is a multifaceted protein that has the potential to modulate multiple pathways in the host cell, including those involved in cell-cycle regulation, RNA splicing and DNA repair.
the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr has a broad range of cellular targets that include proteins involved in cell-cycle regulation, RNA splicing and transcription.
Vpr is a potent regulator of the cellular proteome and phosphoproteome and that it has the potential to regulate a broad range of cellular processes.
